content: Prosthetics and orthotics services should be accessible to individuals of all ages, including children, adults, and older adults. These services must be integrated into the healthcare system or closely connected to it. A three-tiered delivery system is recommended, encompassing primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, with clear referral pathways and follow-up mechanisms. Maintenance and repair services should be an essential component of the prosthetics and orthotics delivery system. In disaster situations, such as natural disasters or armed conflicts, prosthetics and orthotics services are urgently needed. To address these needs effectively, it is crucial to utilize, strengthen, or rebuild local service systems. Coordination among stakeholders is vital to optimize resource use. By integrating prosthetics and orthotics services into health sector responses and encouraging governments to lead coordination efforts, these services can become a permanent part of long-term healthcare strategies. Prosthetics and orthotics services in disaster conditions should be seamlessly integrated into the health sector response, ensuring a smooth transition to long-term service provision. Service units for prosthetics and orthotics should provide a safe, well-equipped environment for professionals and users to interact, design, manufacture, customize, fit, and maintain devices. These units should ideally be located within or closely linked to health and rehabilitation facilities, such as district and referral hospitals, to enhance multidisciplinary collaboration, improve referrals, and expedite treatment. Service units that offer a broader range of assistive devices, including mobility aids like wheelchairs and crutches, as well as vision and hearing devices, can provide cost-effective, comprehensive services to diverse user groups. This approach is particularly beneficial for older populations, who often require multiple types of assistive products. Safety is a critical consideration in prosthetics and orthotics service units. Adherence to occupational health and safety regulations, proper training of personnel, and the use of personal protective equipment (e.g., goggles, masks, gloves) are essential to minimize risks. Systematic monitoring, documentation, and prevention of adverse incidents further enhance safety for both providers and users. The service delivery process for prosthetics and orthotics includes several key steps: assessment, fabrication and fitting, user training, and product delivery with follow-up. Each user should undergo a holistic assessment by a qualified professional or multidisciplinary team, considering their lifestyle, environment, and physical condition. Peer support during service delivery can boost user motivation, accelerate treatment, and improve results. Fabrication and fitting should follow manufacturer guidelines to maximize product potential and minimize hazards. User training, including physiotherapy and occupational therapy, is essential to maximize the benefits of prosthetics and orthotics. Family members and caregivers should also be involved in training, especially for users who rely on regular support. Users and caregivers should have the opportunity to provide feedback during fitting and before finalizing the product. Follow-up is an indispensable part of effective service delivery. Prosthetics and orthotics service providers should establish clear plans for equipment maintenance and replacement. They must also define and adhere to documented health and safety regulations to protect both providers and users. Quality management systems, including clinical audits, are essential for monitoring and improving service and product quality. Feedback from users and caregivers is a valuable tool for measuring quality and enhancing service provision. Strategic planning, monitoring, and evaluation are critical for the development of prosthetics and orthotics services. Annual and long-term plans, supported by performance indicators, provide direction and allow for adjustments to improve outcomes. Member States are encouraged to adapt global standards to their local contexts, prioritizing user rights, safety, quality, and performance. Research and data collection are essential to address gaps in evidence and improve prosthetics and orthotics services. Key research areas include the impact and cost-effectiveness of services, best practices for service delivery, and methods for assessing needs and unmet needs. Collaboration among national and international stakeholders can support research efforts, standardize data collection, and expand the evidence base. Personal stories, such as those of Kirsti in Norway and Dareen in Lebanon, highlight the transformative impact of prosthetics and orthotics on individuals’ lives. These devices enable users to lead active, fulfilling lives, participate in education and employment, and engage in social activities. By improving access to high-quality, affordable prosthetics and orthotics services, we can enhance the health, well-being, and independence of individuals worldwide, contributing to universal health coverage and ensuring that no one is left behind.
